triage.name: Emphysema
triage.reason: Chronic progressive dyspnea with clear risk factors, exam findings and spirometry; overlaps with COPD and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, good teaching case.

demographics: More common in people with a long smoking history
Slightly more common in males in the US, largely reflecting historical smoking patterns

risk_factors.text: Occupational exposure to dusts, fumes, or vapors
Family history of COPD in a smoker
Chronic exposure to indoor or outdoor air pollution

family_history: COPD or emphysema in a first-degree relative
social_history: Long-standing tobacco use, often 20 or more pack-years
Exposure to secondhand smoke at home or work
Work in mining, construction, welding, textiles, or farming

chief_complaints.text: I get winded just walking to the mailbox
I've been short of breath for months and it's getting worse
I can't do the things I used to do
I have this cough that won't go away

hpi.onset: Gradual, over months to years; often attributed at first to getting older or being out of shape
hpi.duration: Usually present for a year or more by the time it is brought to medical attention
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; breathlessness that once appeared only with heavy exertion now comes with walking on flat ground or climbing a short flight of stairs
hpi.location: Chest, felt as breathlessness rather than localized pain
hpi.quality: Air hunger and inability to get a full breath; chest tightness described as a band around the chest
hpi.severity: Mild at first and only with exertion; later moderate to severe, limiting daily activities and sometimes present at rest
hpi.timing: Worse with activity; may be worse in the morning or with cold air and respiratory infections

associated_symptoms.text: Long-standing cough, often bringing up clear or white sputum
Wheezing or a whistling sound when breathing
Decreased ability to exercise or keep up with others
Unintentional weight loss and loss of appetite
Swelling in the ankles or feet

pertinent_negatives: Sudden worsening of breathlessness over hours
Breathlessness that comes in sudden attacks with wheezing that fully resolves
Swelling and pain in one leg
Weight loss with a normal appetite

argues_against: Heart failure as the primary cause

positives.text: Anxiety about not being able to breathe

atypical.how_it_differs: Breathlessness may be blamed on aging or deconditioning, and activity level may already be low, so the disease is often more advanced at diagnosis.

Emphysema is essentially not seen in children; when severe early emphysema occurs it suggests alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or another inherited cause and presents with breathlessness and poor exercise tolerance.
Breathlessness is often attributed to weight, and reduced chest wall compliance can make dyspnea seem out of proportion to the lung findings.
Coexisting heart and kidney disease can mimic or mask the breathlessness and leg swelling of advanced emphysema.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, speaks in full sentences, no distress
general.moderate: Speaks in short sentences, mild tachypnea, prefers sitting upright
general.severe: Pursed-lip breathing, tripod positioning, uses accessory muscles, prolonged expiration
general.critical: Exhausted, diaphoretic, unable to speak in sentences, altered mental status, paradoxical abdominal movement

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest from the side and front
findings.finding: Increased anteroposterior diameter with a barrel-shaped chest

findings.maneuver: Auscultate and time the expiratory phase
findings.finding: Prolonged expiration with a decreased I:E ratio

findings.maneuver: Auscultate during quiet and forced breathing
Observe the neck and chest wall during breathing
findings.finding: Use of sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles
Leaning forward with arms braced on knees or the exam table

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of the feet and ankles
Inspect the lips, oral mucosa, and nail beds
Inspect and palpate the limb musculature
findings.finding: Diffuse muscle wasting, especially of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular venous pulsation at 45 degrees
findings.finding: Jugular venous pressure is not elevated

findings.maneuver: Apply right upper quadrant pressure while watching the jugular vein
Auscultate the apex in the left lateral decubitus position
Compare both calves for size and tenderness
findings.finding: No unilateral calf swelling or tenderness

differential.name: Chronic bronchitis (COPD with chronic bronchitis phenotype)
differential.why_considered: Same exposure history and airflow obstruction; most patients with COPD have features of both

history: Productive cough on most days for at least 3 months a year for 2 or more years
Sputum is prominent and often purulent during exacerbations
Breathlessness may be less prominent early than the cough
exam: Crackles and rhonchi in addition to wheezing
Cyanosis and peripheral edema earlier in the course
labs: Spirometry shows obstruction in both; chronic bronchitis often has more sputum and lower resting oxygen
imaging: Chest x-ray shows increased bronchovascular markings rather than marked hyperinflation

differential.name: Asthma
differential.why_considered: Wheezing, chest tightness and intermittent breathlessness in a patient with cough

history: Symptoms began in childhood or young adulthood
Episodes come in attacks separated by normal periods
Atopy, eczema, allergic rhinitis, or a family history of asthma
Symptoms vary day to day and often wake the patient at night
exam: Wheezing is prominent and reversible; no barrel chest
labs: Spirometry shows obstruction that improves substantially after a bronchodilator
Blood eosinophilia or elevated IgE may be present

differential.name: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
differential.why_considered: Exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, leg swelling and fatigue in an older patient
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, or an S3 gallop

history: Orthopnea and waking at night short of breath
Rapid weight gain from fluid
Known coronary disease or hypertension
exam: Elevated jugular venous pressure, positive hepatojugular reflux, S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles
imaging: Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly, pulmonary venous congestion, and pleural effusions

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Acute worsening of breathlessness in a patient with limited respiratory reserve
differential.trigger: Sudden worsening of dyspnea over hours, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, or unilateral leg swelling

history: Abrupt onset rather than gradual worsening
Recent immobility, surgery, or prior clot
Pleuritic chest pain or hemoptysis
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to the lung findings
labs: Elevated D-dimer; hypoxemia with a widened alveolar-arterial gradient
imaging: CT pulmonary angiography shows a filling defect in the pulmonary arteries
Lower extremity ultrasound may show a deep vein thrombosis

differential.name: Pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: Sudden breathlessness and chest pain in a patient with emphysematous bullae
differential.trigger: Sudden severe one-sided chest pain with acute dyspnea and absent breath sounds on one side

history: Abrupt onset, often at rest
Sharp one-sided chest pain
exam: Absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side
Tracheal deviation and hypotension if tension develops
imaging: Chest x-ray shows a pleural line with no lung markings beyond it

differential.name: Bronchiectasis
differential.why_considered: Chronic productive cough and breathlessness with recurrent chest infections

history: Large volumes of purulent sputum daily
Recurrent pneumonias
History of severe childhood respiratory infection
exam: Coarse crackles, often at the bases
imaging: High-resolution CT shows dilated, thick-walled airways with a signet-ring appearance

differential.name: Lung cancer
differential.why_considered: Long smoking history with cough, breathlessness and weight loss
differential.trigger: Hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, hoarseness, or a new focal finding on chest imaging

history: Hemoptysis
Weight loss with preserved appetite
Hoarseness or bone pain
exam: Focal findings such as unilateral wheeze, decreased breath sounds, or clubbing
labs: Anemia, hypercalcemia, or elevated alkaline phosphatase
imaging: Chest x-ray or CT shows a mass, nodule, or hilar adenopathy
PET-CT and tissue biopsy confirm the diagnosis

differential.name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
differential.why_considered: Emphysema in a younger patient or with a strong family history

history: Symptoms before age 45
Minimal or no smoking history
Family history of early emphysema or liver disease
exam: Signs of liver disease in some patients
labs: Low serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level with a confirmatory genotype or phenotype

severity.mild: Breathlessness only with heavy exertion; FEV1 at or above 80% predicted; comfortable at rest; no hypoxemia
severity.moderate: Breathlessness with walking on flat ground or climbing stairs; FEV1 50-79% predicted; may have chronic cough and sputum; oxygen saturation usually normal at rest
severity.severe: Breathlessness with minimal activity or at rest; FEV1 30-49% predicted; pursed-lip breathing, accessory muscle use, resting hypoxemia possible; frequent exacerbations
severity.critical: Respiratory failure with exhaustion, altered mental status, or hypercapnia; FEV1 below 30% predicted; requires ventilatory support; may be triggered by infection, pneumothorax, or pulmonary embolism

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status, somnolence, or confusion
red_flags.meaning: Hypercapnic respiratory failure; needs urgent blood gas and ventilatory support

red_flags.finding: Unable to speak in full sentences, tripod positioning, accessory muscle use
Sudden severe one-sided chest pain with absent breath sounds
red_flags.meaning: Pneumothorax, possibly tension; needs immediate decompression
Evaluate for lung cancer, bronchiectasis, or infection

red_flags.finding: Unilateral leg swelling with acute dyspnea
red_flags.meaning: Deep vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism

red_flags.finding: Fever with purulent sputum and increased breathlessness
red_flags.meaning: Acute exacerbation, often infectious; consider antibiotics and steroids

red_flags.finding: New peripheral edema with elevated jugular venous pressure
red_flags.meaning: Cor pulmonale or coexisting heart failure

complications.name: Acute exacerbation of COPD
clues: Increased breathlessness and sputum over days
Often triggered by viral or bacterial infection

complications.name: Spontaneous pneumothorax
clues: Absent breath sounds on one side

complications.name: Weight loss and muscle wasting
clues: Loss of appetite and early satiety

complications.name: Osteoporosis
clues: Long-term inhaled or systemic steroid use

special_populations.differences: Breathlessness is often attributed to aging or deconditioning, so the disease is more advanced at diagnosis; more comorbidity and polypharmacy; higher risk of falls and cognitive effects from hypoxemia.
Emphysema is essentially not seen in children; when severe early emphysema occurs it suggests alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or another inherited cause and warrants genetic testing.
Dyspnea may be attributed to normal pregnancy; smoking cessation is the highest priority; hypoxemia threatens both mother and fetus and oxygen targets should be maintained.
Reduced chest wall compliance and weight-related dyspnea can make symptoms seem out of proportion to the lung findings; obesity also increases the work of breathing and complicates inhaler technique.
Coexisting heart and kidney disease can mimic or mask the breathlessness and leg swelling of advanced emphysema; systemic steroids during exacerbations can worsen glycemic control.

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or have you ever smoked? How much and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former cigarette use, usually 20 or more pack-years; the main risk factor

key_questions.question: When did the shortness of breath start, and how has it changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over months to years with slow progression; breathlessness that once came only with heavy exertion now comes with walking on flat ground

key_questions.question: What brings it on or makes it worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertion, cold air, respiratory infections, smoke or fumes; relieved by rest and sitting upright

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough, and do you bring anything up?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-standing cough with clear or white sputum; large volumes of purulent sputum would point elsewhere

key_questions.question: Do you wheeze or feel tightness in your chest?
key_questions.looking_for: Wheezing or a whistling sound and chest tightness

key_questions.question: Have you had any coughing up of blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; hemoptysis raises concern for lung cancer, bronchiectasis, or infection

key_questions.question: Have you had sudden worsening of your breathing or sudden one-sided chest pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; abrupt onset suggests pneumothorax or pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your ankles, feet, or legs?
key_questions.looking_for: New or worsening edema suggesting cor pulmonale or coexisting heart failure

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying, or lost your appetite?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss and early satiety in advanced disease; weight loss with preserved appetite raises concern for cancer

key_questions.question: Do you wake at night short of breath, or need extra pillows to sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea point to heart failure

key_questions.question: Have you had any fevers, chills, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent at baseline; fever with purulent sputum suggests an acute exacerbation

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have emphysema or COPD, especially at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of COPD in a smoker, or early emphysema suggesting alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have asthma, or did your breathing problems start in childhood?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms beginning in childhood or young adulthood with attacks separated by normal periods would suggest asthma instead

key_questions.question: What medicines do you use for your breathing, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Bronchodilators, inhaled steroids, and how well they relieve symptoms

key_questions.question: What kind of work have you done, and were you exposed to dusts, fumes, or chemicals?
key_questions.looking_for: Mining, construction, welding, textiles, or farming exposures that contribute to lung damage

key_questions.question: Does anyone smoke in your home or workplace?

reasoning_points: Gradual, progressive exertional dyspnea over months to years in a patient over 40
Substantial smoking history or other long-term inhaled irritant exposure
Chronic cough with scant sputum, wheezing, and chest tightness
Exam findings of hyperinflation: barrel chest, hyperresonance, diffusely decreased breath sounds, prolonged expiration
Spirometry showing persistent airflow obstruction that does not fully reverse with a bronchodilator
Chest imaging showing hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms
Heart failure and pulmonary embolism considered and argued against by the absence of orthopnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, S3 gallop, and unilateral leg swelling
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency considered if symptoms began before age 45 or with minimal smoking history

easy: Older adult with a long smoking history
Classic gradual exertional dyspnea with chronic cough
Barrel chest, hyperresonance, and decreased breath sounds
medium: Older adult whose breathlessness is attributed to aging or deconditioning
Coexisting heart failure with leg swelling and crackles
Obesity with dyspnea out of proportion to the lung findings
Prominent chronic bronchitis features with purulent sputum
hard: Younger patient with minimal smoking history suggesting alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Acute exacerbation with hypercapnia and altered mental status
Sudden worsening from pneumothorax or pulmonary embolism
Weight loss and hemoptysis raising concern for lung cancer
